sat.title: How We Say Things
sat.transcript:
cast: lehua, derek, sarah, pono, kaden
LEHUA: Aloha, and welcome to SAT Notes. I'm Lehua, and before we teach you one single thing about the SAT, we gotta do something more important. We gotta agree on how we say stuff.
KADEN: Wait, this is the pronunciation episode? I thought we were doing math.
DEREK: We are doing math, Kaden. Episode four. This is episode zero.
KADEN: There's an episode zero?
SARAH: There's always an episode zero. It's like the preface of a book. Everybody skips it, and then they mispronounce everything for the rest of their life.
LEHUA: So here's the deal. This show is made on Hawaiʻi Island, for Hawaiʻi Island kids. We're gonna say place names the way they're actually said, and we're gonna say the test names the way the test people say them. Coach, you want to start us off?
PONO: Shoots. Hawaiʻi. Not "Huh-why-ee." Hah-VAI-ee. Four little syllables and that ʻokina in the middle, that little catch, like you forgot something.
KADEN: Hah-VAI-ee.
PONO: There you go. Waimea. Wy-MAY-ah. Where this show lives. Where I was born, where my horse was born, where my horse's horse was born.
SARAH: That's not how horses work, Coach.
PONO: You don't know my horses.
LEHUA: Kohala. Koh-HAH-lah. The mountain behind us. Mauna Kea. MOW-nah KEH-ah. Not "Mona Kaya." If you say Mona Kaya on this show, Derek will rate you.
DEREK: Four out of ten.
KADEN: Harsh.
DEREK: It's generous.
SARAH: Let's do the towns, because you're all from somewhere. Hilo. HEE-loh. Honokaʻa. Hoh-noh-KAH-ah. Kealakehe. Keh-ah-lah-KEH-heh. Konawaena. Koh-nah-WY-nah.
KADEN: Konawaena always gets me. Koh-nah-WY-nah.
SARAH: Good. Pāhoa. PAH-hoh-ah. Keaʻau. Keh-ah-AH-oo. Kaʻū. Kah-OO. Waiākea. Wy-AH-keh-ah. And Laupāhoehoe. Lau-PAH-hoy-hoy.
PONO: Laupāhoehoe is a test by itself.
LEHUA: And some words we'll use a lot. Kumu. KOO-moo. That's a teacher. Akamai. Ah-kah-MY. That's smart, which is what you're going to be. Pau. Pow. That's done, finished. Pau hana, pow HAH-nah, that's done with work. Kōkua, KOH-koo-ah, help. And our name. Alakaʻi. Ah-lah-KAH-ee. It means to lead, to guide. Which is the whole point. We're not here to drag you through this test. You're leading. We're just the guides.
KADEN: Okay but I came for the acronyms. What is an S-A-T even.
DEREK: SAT. Say the letters. Ess, ay, tee. It used to stand for something. It doesn't anymore. The company that makes it, College Board, says it just stands for SAT now.
KADEN: That's so unserious.
DEREK: Agreed. Eight out of ten for honesty though.
SARAH: PSAT. Pee, ess, ay, tee. The practice one. Sometimes you'll see PSAT slash NMSQT. En, em, ess, kyoo, tee. National Merit Scholarship Qualifying Test. You do not need to say that out loud ever again. Just know that the PSAT you take junior year can get you scholarship money.
LEHUA: ACT. Ay, see, tee. The other test. We have a whole other show for that one. Same people, different hat.
PONO: I only got the one hat.
LEHUA: We'll get you a second hat, Coach.
DEREK: A few more. The SAT now is digital, so some people call it the DSAT, dee ess ay tee. Same test. And the two halves are Reading and Writing, which the nerds write as R W, and Math, which the nerds write as Math.
SARAH: The nerds being us.
DEREK: Correct.
KADEN: What about Bluebook? My counselor keeps saying Bluebook.
SARAH: Bluebook is the app you take the real SAT on. Blue book, two words, one app. It's also where the free official practice tests live. We'll say it a lot. And Khan Academy, con academy, that's the free official practice site. Those two plus this show plus the drills in the app, and you don't need to buy anything.
LEHUA: One more. HPA. Aitch, pee, ay. Hawaiʻi Preparatory Academy, up the road. The kid who built the app we're sitting inside of goes there. So if the app ever looks a little red and white by default, now you know why. You can pick your own school and it changes colors.
KADEN: Can I make it Konawaena green?
LEHUA: Koh-nah-WY-nah green. Yes.
PONO: Alright. That's how we say things. Now when I tell you the clock is a horse and you gotta ride it, not fight it, you'll know I said it in Wy-MAY-ah.
SARAH: And when I correct your commas, you'll know it's with aloha.
DEREK: And when I rate your shortcut a six, it's a good six.
KADEN: Is anything ever a ten?
DEREK: Not yet.
LEHUA: That's episode zero. Episode one is how this test actually works, which is less scary than you think. Go do three drills in the app, come back, we'll be here. Mahalo, and I gotta go to Costco.
KADEN: It's Tuesday.
LEHUA: Costco doesn't care what day it is.

check.q: How is the name of this app, Alakaʻi, pronounced?
What does SAT stand for today, according to College Board?
Which app do you take the real digital SAT on?

sat.title: The Time Squeeze
sat.transcript:
cast: lehua, pono, derek, kaden
LEHUA: Aloha, SAT Notes, episode three. I'm Lehua. Today is the one everybody asks about. The clock. Coach Pono is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here looking like he already ran out of time.
KADEN: I was up late. The bus was early. It's a whole thing.
PONO: Kaden, that's the episode. You ran out of time before the test started. Welcome.
LEHUA: So, Coach, set it up. Why does the clock feel like it's attacking people?
PONO: Because they treat it like a bull. They fight it. You cannot fight a clock. The clock is a horse. You don't beat a horse, you ride it. You set a pace, you check it twice, and you don't let it decide where you're going.
DEREK: I'm going to say the actual numbers now, because Coach is going to keep saying horse.
PONO: I'm gonna keep saying horse.
DEREK: Reading and Writing. Two modules. Each one is twenty-seven questions in thirty-two minutes. That's about seventy-one seconds a question. Math. Two modules. Twenty-two questions in thirty-five minutes. About ninety-five seconds a question.
KADEN: Seventy-one seconds is nothing.
DEREK: Seventy-one seconds is plenty if you don't spend four minutes on question nine.
LEHUA: And that's the real problem, right? Nobody runs out of time evenly. They run out because of two or three questions that ate everything.
PONO: Exactly. The clock didn't beat you. One question beat you, and then the clock just told you about it.
KADEN: Okay so what do I actually do.
PONO: Two passes. First pass, you ride through in order. You look at a question. If you can see the path in about ten seconds, you take it. If you can't see the path, you pick your best guess, you flag it, and you move on. You do not sit there. Sitting there is fighting the horse.
KADEN: But what if I almost have it.
DEREK: "Almost have it" is the most expensive phrase on the SAT. Almost have it for one more minute is three questions you never saw. Those three could be easy. The one you're stuck on, by definition, is not.
LEHUA: And when you guess, cross things out first. The app has a little x next to every choice. Use it.
DEREK: Right. Crossing out one wrong choice turns a one-in-four guess into one-in-three. Cross out two and it's a coin flip. Small moves, real points. One warning: only cross out a choice when you can say why it is wrong. If you cross out the right answer, the app will tell you, and that's a sign you were guessing with the x button, not thinking with it.
LEHUA: Say the guessing rule, Derek, because people still don't believe it.
DEREK: There is no guessing penalty. None. On the SAT and on the ACT. A blank is a guaranteed zero. A random guess on a four-choice question is worth a quarter of a point on average. And if you can cross out even one wrong choice, it's a third. So a blank is the only answer that is always wrong.
KADEN: So I should just guess on everything?
DEREK: You should answer everything. Guessing is what you do when you've run out of better options. But the rule is, no blanks. Ever. Pau. Done.
PONO: Second pass. You got time left, you go back to the flags. You already have an answer on every one of them, so you're not rescuing anything, you're just upgrading. Start with the one that looked closest. Leave the monster for last. If the clock runs out while you're on the monster, who cares, you already answered it.
LEHUA: And on the digital SAT the flag is built in. There's a button. And there's a little grid at the bottom that shows you every question and whether you answered it. Use the grid. That's your dashboard.
KADEN: What about checkpoints? My tutor said something about checkpoints.
PONO: Your tutor's right. You look at the clock exactly twice. Not every thirty seconds. Twice. At the one-third mark and the two-thirds mark. And you ask one question. Am I at or past the target?
DEREK: Reading and Writing, that's question nine at ten minutes forty, and question eighteen at twenty-one minutes twenty. Math, question seven at eleven forty, and question fifteen at twenty-three twenty. Those are in the app on the Time Squeeze page, you don't have to memorize them right now.
PONO: If you're behind, you flag faster. That's it. You don't panic, you don't speed-read, you just lower the bar for what you'll flag. If you're ahead, you slow down one notch. Being ahead means you're probably rushing.
KADEN: Being ahead is bad?
PONO: Being ahead on a horse means the horse is running you.
LEHUA: Let's talk about what happens in the last sixty seconds, because that's where people lose points they already had.
DEREK: In the last minute, you stop solving. Full stop. You open the grid, you look for anything unanswered, and you put something in. Then you stop. A half-finished solution is worth zero. A guess is worth something.
KADEN: What if I'm in the middle of a question and I have it?
DEREK: If you have it, you have it. Finish it, then check the grid. But "I have it" means you're writing the answer, not "I think I see where this goes."
LEHUA: Okay, Kaden, you're the one who actually takes this thing. What goes wrong for you?
KADEN: Honestly? Reading. I get into a passage and I read the whole thing like it's a book. Then the question is about one sentence and I'm like, I don't remember that sentence.
LEHUA: Yeah, that's the number one time leak in Reading and Writing. The digital SAT gives you one short passage per question. One. It's not a long passage with ten questions. So the move is, read the question first, then read the passage knowing what you're hunting for.
PONO: Read the brand before you buy the cow.
KADEN: Coach, what.
PONO: Know what you're looking for before you look.
DEREK: Math version. Read the last sentence of the word problem first. That's the actual question. Then read the rest to collect the numbers. You'll stop doing arithmetic you didn't need.
KADEN: Okay that one's actually good.
DEREK: Seven out of ten.
KADEN: Why not higher?
DEREK: Nothing's higher.
LEHUA: One more thing and then we'll let Kaden go catch his bus. The adaptive thing. The SAT is adaptive by module. Module one is the same difficulty for everybody. Depending on how you do, module two is either the harder version or the easier version, and the harder version can score higher. So what does that mean for the clock?
DEREK: It means module one accuracy matters more than module one speed. Do not sprint module one to save time. There's no saving time, each module has its own clock. Get module one right, calmly, and you unlock the module that can give you the big score.
PONO: Ride the first horse clean. Then they give you the fast horse.
KADEN: There it is.
LEHUA: Alright. Here's your homework. If you haven't done the placement check yet, do that first, it's two questions per skill and it tells the dashboard where to start you. Then go to Timed in the app. Do one Reading and Writing module, just one, with the checkpoints on. Don't worry about the score. Watch what the clock does to you. Then come back and do episode four.
KADEN: And flag stuff.
PONO: And flag stuff. No blanks.
DEREK: No blanks.
LEHUA: No blanks. That's SAT Notes. Mahalo, go catch your bus, Kaden.
KADEN: It left.
PONO: Should've flagged it.

check.q: Is there a guessing penalty on the SAT?
choices: Yes, a quarter point per wrong answer
No, a blank is the only answer that is always wrong

check.q: In the two-pass method, what do you do with a question you cannot see the path on in about ten seconds?
choices: Keep working until you get it
Leave it blank and move on
Pick your best guess, flag it, move on
Skip to the end of the module

check.q: How many times should you check the clock during a module?
choices: Twice, at the one-third and two-thirds marks
